visualization.description: For the illustrated refund, start with Postgres: related customer balance, refund and approval records can commit in one transaction. A support-case document groups messages, proposal and review state, but a separately stored balance needs an explicit cross-document design. title: Should a security fix wait for the next feature release?
seoTitle: Production-led security maintenance: patching live apps between releases
excerpt: A finished app still needs repairs. Patch it from production, carry the fix back to development, and refuse any later release that would undo it.
shareLine: A security fix is finished when it survives the next release.

proof.heading: Will the repair survive the next release?
proof.description: An illustrative booking API: production is repaired from its own release, a newer feature build still carries the old parser, and the deployment gate decides whether the fix survives.
proof.label: See where it sits in Orchestra OS

image.alt: Connected wireframe shield, wrench, clock forms in Orchestra's mesh style.
image.caption: Editorial mesh illustration · Explore the workflow in the article.

headerImage.alt: Connected wireframe shield, wrench, clock forms in Orchestra's mesh style.

visualization.takeaway: A security fix is finished when it survives the next release.
visualization.description: A worked example with an illustrative booking API. Production runs release A while development has moved on to branch B; when the bundled HTTP parser needs a security fix, maintenance builds A + fix from production and ships it through the deployment gate, which records the parser fix as required. A later build from B is newer and passes its tests but still carries the old parser: a gate that checks required fixes refuses it and assigns an owner to carry the fix into B, while a gate that checks release order alone admits it and production runs the vulnerable parser again.

figures.title: Where does the effort go?
figures.takeaway: Scan what customers use. Repair it there first.
figures.description: One advisory for the HTTP parser in the booking API travels through two flows at the same pace. Through the dev loop, scanners on four environments raise four alerts (three on servers no customer touches), and the fix passes six hands-on steps, including review, staging sign-off and a change approval that waits for the release window: production is protected at step 8 of 8. Production-led sweeps what is live, raises one finding with one owner, repairs the running release within agreed policy and verifies it in service: production is protected at step 4 of 5, with the fix carried back to development afterwards while CI keeps its pre-release checks.

sources.label: Amazon Inspector: rescanning images for new vulnerabilities

figures.takeaway: What one app learns, every app on the platform gets.

title: We got our first PR merged into OpenTelemetry
seoTitle: OpenTelemetry GenAI conversation ID: passing it to nested spans
excerpt: OpenTelemetry's GenAI conventions now say how an agent framework can share its conversation ID with the model and tool calls nested inside it. Review narrowed the rule to that one ID; agent naming continues in a separate draft.
shareLine: OpenTelemetry's GenAI conventions now let model and tool calls inside an agent record its conversation ID.
invite: Bring an agent workflow you need to trace. We'll look at what each span should record and where the conversation and agent identities belong.

proof.heading: Follow one conversation
proof.description: Pull request #556 to OpenTelemetry's GenAI semantic conventions, merged 30 October 2026 after two approvals from reviewers at different companies. Merged on main; no tagged release yet.
proof.label: Read the merged pull request

image.alt: Connected wireframe conversation, magnifier, gift forms in Orchestra's mesh style.
image.caption: Editorial mesh illustration · Explore the workflow in the article.

visualization.takeaway: One conversation ID, carried from the agent into the model and tool calls nested inside it.
visualization.description: An illustrative trace of one support conversation in one process. Without propagation, only spans whose own library knows the conversation record its ID, so a query by conversation finds three of six spans. With the rule, the agent framework passes the ID in context and the nested model calls record it too. A remote agent's library has its own session ID, and that value wins. The token metric never carries the ID because GenAI metrics don't reference it. The third view shows why agent names stayed out of the list: inherited, the remote agent's span would name its caller.
visualization.evidenceLabel: Illustrative trace · rules quoted from the merged section

figures.title: Where the rule sits
figures.takeaway: Thirty reference libraries write to the same conventions; six record the conversation ID in their scenarios. Seven backends group conversations by it.
figures.description: The GenAI semantic conventions sit between the libraries that write telemetry and the backends that read it. The repository's reference scenarios check 30 Python libraries: 11 model clients, 12 agent frameworks, five hosted agents or agent protocols and two evaluation libraries (grouping ours). In those scenarios, six libraries record gen_ai.conversation.id on at least one span: adk_a2a, agent-framework, google-adk, openai-assistants, aws-bedrock-agent and a2a-python. By span: agent invocation inside the process 2 of 8 libraries, remote agent invocation 2 of 4, workflow 1 of 4, inference 2 of 14, tool execution 2 of 11, A2A client and server 1 of 1 each: 11 of 43 in all. Scenario coverage shows what each reference scenario exercises, not everything a library can do. On the reading side, 14 backends document reading the GenAI conventions. Datadog, Honeycomb, Grafana Cloud, Dynatrace, Opik, W&B Weave and Pydantic Logfire document grouping an agent conversation by gen_ai.conversation.id; Langfuse, Arize Phoenix, MLflow, LangSmith, Braintrust, New Relic and Google Cloud document reading the conventions. Backend documentation read 30 October 2026; no endorsement or partnership is implied.

figures.description: Opened on 1 October as an 18-line summary of where gen_ai.agent.name and gen_ai.conversation.id appear. On 12 October Liudmila Molkova asked for normative guidance, proposed its wording and asked for links to canonical definitions; the revision was approved the next day. The repository requires a second approval from another company for non-editorial changes. On 23 October Trask Stalnaker showed how an inherited agent name can identify the wrong agent; the GenAI SIG continued agent naming in #385, and the agent name was removed on 27 October. Trask approved on 30 October with two wording suggestions, both applied, and Liudmila approved and merged the change at 22:56 UTC.
